The answer is false. The hyperchromic effect predicts that the concentration of dsDNA must be greater.  The hyperchromic effect is the increase in UV absorbance of DNA when it is denatured from dsDNA to ssDNA. This is because the bases in the double stranded DNA are stacked on top of each other, which restricts the movement of the electron clouds of the bases and thus reduces the absorbance of UV light. When the DNA is denatured, the two strands are separated and the bases are no longer stacked on top of each other. This allows the electron clouds of the bases to move freely and thus increases the absorbance of UV light. Therefore, in order for the UV absorbance of dsDNA and ssDNA to be the same, the concentration of ssDNA must be half that of dsDNA.

This is because the Renilla luciferase levels will still be impacted by transfection efficiency, the number of cells in each well and the amount of time each sample is incubated. The first half of the statement is true, as the strength of the promoter sequence is indeed dependent upon its resemblance of the consensus sequence. However, the second half of the statement is false, as the strength of the promoter sequence does not dictate the length of the DNA segment that will be transcribed into RNA molecules. Instead, the length of the DNA segment that will be transcribed into RNA molecules is determined by the position of the transcription start site and the position of the terminator sequence.
